Article Title: Multiple Indian payloads reach orbit aboard SpaceX’s Falcon 9
Article Text:
SpaceX Falcon 9 launches multiple Indian payloads into orbit (representational image)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

BENGALURU: Multiple Indian payloads, representing four space startups, reached orbit aboard SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket, which lifted off at 12:02 am IST on Friday (October 2) as part of the Transporter-18 rideshare mission.The mission carried satellites developed by Dhruva Space and TakeMe2Space, along with payloads from SatLeo Labs and EON Space Labs. The payloads will demonstrate technologies for thermal imaging, Earth observation and artificial intelligence (AI)-based data processing in orbit.Dhruva’s LEAP-2 satellite, its second commercial mission using the P-30 satellite platform, was successfully deployed into orbit at 1 am IST. It hosts two in-orbit demonstration payloads: a star tracker developed by France-based Sodern, part of ArianeGroup, and TAPAS-1, developed by SatLeo Labs.SatLeo describes TAPAS-1, or Thermal Access Platform for Analytics & Solutions, as India’s first dedicated commercial thermal payload. The CubeSat-category payload uses thermal infrared sensing to capture temperature information that conventional optical satellite imagery cannot directly provide.The mission will validate its thermal sensing technology, payload performance and data-processing capabilities in orbit.“Most satellites show us what the Earth looks like, TAPAS-1 will show us how it behaves by revealing temperature patterns that ordinary payloads cannot see,” said Shravan Bhati, co-founder and CEO, SatLeo Labs.Dhruva Space also undertook the end-to-end integration of LEAP-2 with the Falcon 9 launch vehicle. The company said this builds on its work on LEAP-1, through which it became the first Indian private company to undertake the launch vehicle integration of its satellite in-house.“This extends our role beyond satellite manufacturing into launch integration and end-to-end mission delivery, reinforcing its full-stack Space engineering approach. LEAP-2 will also be supported by our growing global ground infrastructure, including its owned and operated ground station in Luleå, Sweden; the first non-govt entity owned and operated ground station outside India, authorised by the GoI to provide Ground-Station-as-a-Service,” the firm added.TakeMe2Space’s 14-kg MOI-1A satellite is designed to allow customers to run AI models on Earth-observation data directly in orbit. It carries onboard computing capacity of 117 trillion operations per second (TOPS), 2 TB of storage and a nine-band multispectral imager. Processing imagery in space could reduce the need to transmit large volumes of raw data to Earth, with potential applications in agriculture, mining and supply-chain intelligence.MOI-1A follows TakeMe2Space’s 2024 MOI-TD technology demonstration, which validated onboard AI inference and data processing. The company said it had signed up 23 customers for its in-orbit inference services.MOI-1A also carried MIRA, a 502-g optical telescope developed by EON Space Labs. “A compact optical telescope engineered for space imaging. It delivers high-resolution Earth observation with exceptional stability and thermal robustness,” EON describes the payload.MIRA is a pathfinder for a planned small satellite constellation. Its flight comes after the loss of the PSLV-C62 mission on Jan 12, which had affected the company’s earlier launch plans.“Satellites collect vast amounts of data, but much of it still has to reach the ground before it can be turned into useful information. With MOI-1A, customers will be able to run their AI models directly in orbit and receive the insights they need, without downloading all the raw imagery. This mission is an important step towards making computing in space a service that businesses can use,” Ronak Kumar Samantray, founder and CEO, TakeMe2Space, said.
Article Summary: Multiple Indian payloads, representing four space startups, reached orbit aboard SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket. The mission carried satellites developed by Dhruva Space and TakeMe2Space, along with payloads from SatLeo Labs and EON Space Labs. The payloads will demonstrate technologies for thermal imaging, Earth observation and artificial intelligence-based data processing in orbit.

Article Title: How India's classrooms are coping in the age of instant gratification & low attention spans
Article Text:
Representative image.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Classrooms in parts of India are grappling with an underlying problem that no curriculum revision can easily fix. Students raised on on-demand food delivery, constant social media reels and instant AI answers are finding it harder to sustain attention, tolerate boredom, or work toward rewards that don't arrive at once.Teachers, as a result, are increasingly engaging a generation that is much less attentive than before. A recent nationwide survey by the National Council of CBSE Schools found that almost 70% of teachers across the country have observed a sharp decline in their students' focus and classroom attention.The survey, which covered around 6.3 lakh respondents -- teachers, under 18 students and their parents -- also found that 74% of students spend more than two hours a day on screen for non-academic purposes. And teachers reported rising anxiety, irritability and reduced face-to-face interaction among children.Parmeshwar Dattarao Bhurke, a teacher, says the trend is evident in everyday classroom experiences. "Many children no longer have the focus needed to sit through an hour-long lesson or read a passage without their minds wandering," he said. This has prompted many teachers to experiment with newer learning methods, he added."Earlier, one student could read a chapter aloud while the rest of the class listened. That no longer works. .. The idea now is to keep their minds actively engaged through the session."Priya, another middle school teacher, says she has noticed a decline in students' retention levels. "Even when children appear to be listening, their minds are elsewhere. They are also less willing to struggle through any difficult task. This affects their performance in school as well as their behaviour, as they become averse to any kind of challenges or discomfort."For 15-year-old student Chinmayee Sonna, the shift is visible in the way her classmates now study. "Instead of sitting with textbooks or working through ideas, many of my classmates look for the easier option, whether that is AI-generated summaries or explainer videos. They are able to retain less through this method but it helps revise quickly and saves time," she said.Psychologists say such habits reflect a behavioural shift driven by constant access to instant rewards. "They trigger dopamine, giving us a brief rush of joy that reinforces the behaviour and makes us want to repeat it. This is different from the real-life feats, where satisfaction comes only after much effort and patience," Rashi Bhatnagar, a psychologist, said.It is these consequences that extend into the classroom. "When rewards come with almost no effort, the brain begins to prefer them. Like an unused muscle, our ability to wait, tolerate boredom and sustain attention gradually weakens, leaving us restless when tasks demand patience," Bhatnagar said.This is why there is a downside to schools trying to make every lesson entertaining, she adds. "Education cannot always provide instant pleasure if it is to encourage deep thinking. Schools need to consciously create opportunities for children to reflect and generate new ideas."The habit of expecting immediate outcomes also affects resilience. "Because children have not developed the ability to wait for results, many give up too quickly. We need to teach them not to quit at the first sign of difficulty," Bhatnagar said.Psychiatrist Nisha Singla, talking about the digital ecosystem, says it is deliberately designed to reinforce instant gratification. "Social media apps, notifications and quick commerce applications are addictive and the brain begins to crave them. Reading or learning something new also gives us a sense of achievement, but the reward is delayed. That is where all the difference lies."Rebuilding patience, she says, begins with allowing children to slow down. "We need to let them get bored... There is a tendency to fill every moment of their day with something or the other, but boredom is equally important. Parents and schools should consciously encourage delayed gratification."Another challenge to consider in adapting classrooms is large class sizes and poor teacher-student ratios. "This leaves little room for us to nurture each child's curiosity and individual learning needs. At the same time, schools remain under pressure to deliver high marks and pass percentages, leaving us focused on examination outcomes rather than redesigning learning around children's changing needs," Priya said.As educators wait for the national mental health and well-being policy for schools, they say it should help students find meaning in a learning process whose greatest rewards cannot be a sprint and a quick fix.
Article Summary: Students raised on on-demand food delivery, constant social media reels are finding it harder to sustain attention, tolerate boredom, or work toward rewards that don't arrive at once. A recent nationwide survey by the National Council of CBSE Schools found that almost 70% of teachers across the country have observed a sharp decline in their students' focus.

Article Title: 'He has good ideas': Putin lauds PM Modi's peace push to end Russia-Ukraine war
Article Text:
Putin says PM Modi ‘constantly raises’ need to end Ukraine conflict

Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday lauded Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s efforts to seek an end to the Ukraine conflict, saying that he has “good ideas” for achieving a peaceful resolution."Prime Minister Narendra Modi is one of those world leaders who, despite our very good and even friendly relations, personal good relations, constantly raises the question and asks the question about putting an end to the conflict in Ukraine," Putin said.Asked about the issue at the Valdai Club forum, Putin said Prime Minister Narendra Modi has been actively working to find mutually acceptable solutions to the Ukraine conflict."He has an avid interest and very good ideas aimed at finding mutually acceptable solutions. In that sense, naturally, the Prime Minister takes a neutral position but with an interest in the end of the conflict. I think it's my duty to say that directly. And we are thankful to the Prime Minister for his ideas," Putin said.Putin thanked PM Modi for his efforts and continued support for resolving the Ukraine conflict through dialogue."We are thankful for his desire to put an end to this conflict through peaceful means and as soon as possible," he added.Prime Minister Modi and Putin last met in September on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, where they discussed strengthening trade ties, including the implementation of the Programme for Economic Cooperation 2030, along with cooperation in infrastructure, energy, technology, defence and culture.PM Modi has repeatedly called for peace, stressing that India has maintained a principled and humanitarian approach to the Russia-Ukraine conflict."India has maintained a principled and humanitarian stance on the conflict which is equally appreciated by both President Putin and President Zelenskyy. In line with this, both the leaders spoke to me to share their perspectives on the developments related to the conflict. I reiterated India's principled and consistent stand and encouraged dialogue and diplomacy to resolve the conflict," the Prime Minister said during an interview with Japanese news outlet 'The Yomiuri Shimbun' while on a visit to the country in August.Responding to a question on India’s role in peace efforts between the two countries, Prime Minister Modi said, "I have already indicated India's willingness to support meaningful efforts aimed at achieving a peaceful resolution of the conflict. I believe, by virtue of our good relations with both sides, including key stakeholders, we can strengthen efforts dedicated to the restoration of an early and lasting peace in Ukraine. "This comes as Putin reiterated Moscow’s long-standing position that Russia has no plans to attack European countries, while warning that it would respond to any aggression with “all weapons” at its disposal.He also accused Western countries, particularly in Europe, of escalating tensions by discussing preparations for a possible war with Moscow, conducting military drills in the Baltic Sea and seizing Russian vessels.European leaders and intelligence agencies have warned that Russia could be capable of launching an attack on another country within the next few years, particularly if it emerges victorious from the war in Ukraine.
Article Summary: Putin says PM Modi ‘constantly raises’ need to end Ukraine conflict. PM Modi has repeatedly called for peace, stressing that India has maintained a principled and humanitarian approach to the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Putin reiterated Moscow’s long-standing position that Russia has no plans to attack European countries, while warning that it would respond to any aggression with “all weapons”

Article Title: No uniform explanation for collegium decisions on compassionate transfers
Article Text:
The five-member collegium on Sept 28 recommended the repatriation of Justice T Vinod Kumar from Madras HC to his parent HC in Telangana 'in view of his ensuing retirement on Nov 16'

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court collegium's decisions to transfer judges from one HC to another are explained as being meant "for the better administration of justice". But the standard reasoning does not translate into a uniform explanation, with the collegium showing unusual compassion in approving requests from some for transfer or repatriation due to difficult family situations or health issues, while maintaining aloofness from others.There are many judges in HCs who have expressed resentment at the absence of any procedure or norm for transfer of HC judges. A member of the collegium, who will go on to become CJI, has mooted framing a transparent transfer policy. He told TOI that a judge under consideration for transfer should be warned first to mend his ways and be kept under watch for some time. Only when he does not improve should he be transferred, he said.The five-member collegium on Sept 28 recommended the repatriation of Justice T Vinod Kumar from Madras HC to his parent HC in Telangana "in view of his ensuing retirement on Nov 16". Justice Kumar was transferred from Telangana HC to Madras HC in May last year by the SC collegium headed by then CJI BR Gavai.In May last year, a complaint had reached the SC alleging that Justice Kumar, heading a division bench, had kept more than 50 judgments reserved.Sitting as a single judge, he had reserved verdicts in over 170 cases since 2020. If Justice Kumar's imminent retirement was a ground for his repatriation, no such consideration was shown to Justice D Nagarjun, who was transferred from Telangana HC to Madras HC. Justice Nagarjun, a career judicial officer who was elevated as an HC judge in March 2022, was transferred to Madras HC in April 2023.As he was due to retire on Aug 14, 2024, he sent a request to the CJI on July 25, 2024, for repatriation to his parent HC in Telangana, but the collegium remained aloof to the request and allowed him to retire in Madras HC.A Punjab and Haryana HC judge represented against his transfer to another HC, citing his wife's serious illness and disability of his child. But that evoked no compassion with the collegium, which remained firm on his transfer.Justice D V Ramana, who was only 13 years old when his railway gangman father died in an accident, rose from humble backgrounds to become a judge of Andhra Pradesh HC in Aug 2022. He was transferred to Madhya Pradesh HC in Nov 2023. On his retirement in May last year, he gave vent to his frustration. He said he was asked for options and chose Karnataka HC to enable better treatment for his wife, who had a neurological disorder. But that was not heeded. He again requested a transfer to Karnataka to help his wife get treated at Nimhans but that was neither considered nor rejected.
Article Summary: The five-member collegium on Sept 28 recommended the repatriation of Justice T Vinod Kumar from Madras HC to his parent HC in Telangana. If Justice Kumar's imminent retirement was a ground for his repatriation, no such consideration was shown to Justice D Nagarjun. A member of the collegium, who will go on to become CJI, has mooted framing a transparent transfer policy.

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday rejected a petition by Mamata Banerjee-headed TMC faction seeking de-freezing of its three bank accounts on grounds that the party required funds to carry out political activities, such as holding rallies and meetings.Challenging Calcutta HC's order allowing only meeting of day-to-day expenses of the party from these accounts, senior advocate A M Singhvi said the party's three Indian Bank accounts, which have been given a clean chit by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) in a separate proceeding, should be allowed to be operated by the party.Solicitor general Tushar Mehta, appearing for West Bengal govt, told a bench of Justices M M Sundresh and P B Varale that the accounts in question are frozen based on the FIR lodged by the state police, as there is evidence that Rs 35 crore, generated from the fraudulent sale of government land after it was misrepresented as private land by Abhishek Banerjee's PS Sumit Roy, was deposited in these bank accounts.Mehta also mentioned there is a plea pending before the EC as to which is the real TMC, the faction headed by Mamata or the rival group, adding that the EC has frozen the party symbol and allotted both factions ad hoc symbols to contest bypolls.The bench said it would not examine merits of the case as it is l pending with HC, which in the interim has already rejected the plea for de-freezing the accounts. It requested the HC to expedite adjudication of the pending petition on the issue.In its petition, the Mamata faction said it urgently required funds to meet expenses that would arise from preparations for the bypolls.Referring to an earlier ED proceeding freezing its three HDFC bank accounts, TMC said, "The FIR does not pertain to its Indian Bank accounts as no transaction is linked to the four bank accounts to the alleged offence.Successive and progressive freezing of TMC's bank accounts indicates mala fide use of power by state authorities to paralyse operations of a nationally recognised party."
Article Summary: Supreme Court rejects petition by Mamata Banerjee-headed TMC faction seeking de- freezing of its three bank accounts. In its petition, the Mamata faction said it urgently required funds to meet expenses that would arise from preparations for bypolls.

Article Text:
PFRDA expects 2-3 crore new NPS subscribers over next two years

NEW DELHI: The Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) is preparing a roadmap to allow entities regulated by it to invest directly in large infrastructure projects, beyond the current mechanism of investing through ReITS, InVITS and alternate investment funds (AIFs), chairman S Raman told TOI."A committee has been set up to look at the issue, and internal discussions are under way to evolve a mechanism where PFRDA can invest directly in such projects. It will be long, patient capital and may be possible at least five years down the line," said Raman on the sidelines of an event on NPS Diwas.Globally, Canadian pension funds are known to invest directly in big infra projects, including in India, and they hold a significant stake in such projects, including through equity. "All such modalities are being looked into," said Raman.At the event, financial services secretary Sanjay Lohiya said that as the domestic "pension kitty" grows, people are hopeful that a lot of long-term investment, particularly in infrastructure, will be provided by these pension funds."Risk, reward and the quality of investment have to be kept in mind, but govt and other stakeholders are hopeful that slowly our pension funds will be able to provide patient capital."The officer also said that despite the government introducing the Unified Pension Scheme (UPS), which provides an assured and inflation-indexed monthly pension equivalent to 50% of the average basic pay drawn in the last 12 months, most employees covered under NPS "choose" not to opt for the scheme.Raman also said that PFRDA is stepping up efforts to expand NPS beyond govt employees and the corporate sector, with focus on informal workers, self-employed people and small business owners. "PFRDA aims to add two to three crore subscribers to the NPS in the next two years."
Article Summary: Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) is preparing a roadmap to allow entities regulated by it to invest directly in large infrastructure projects. PFRDA expects 2-3 crore new NPS subscribers over next two years. Canadian pension funds are known to investment directly in big infra projects, including in India.
